title: California's Governor Primary Remains Undecided as Becerra and Hilton Lead a Crowded Field
summary: California's primary election for governor remained undecided Wednesday, with vote counting continuing in a race that featured 60 candidates vying for the state's top job. Democrat Xavier Becerra, a former U.S. Health and Human Services secretary, and Republican business executive Steve Hilton led the field, while Democratic billionaire activist Tom Steyer was in third place. Under California's unusual primary system, all candidates appear on a single ballot open to any registered voter, and the top two finishers advance to the general election—even if they're from the same party. Becerra's lead marks a dramatic comeback. As recently as April, polls showed him languishing in single digits. At his Los Angeles watch party, he embraced his underdog status. 'Here in Hollywood's hometown, we love a good underdog success story,' he said, comparing his campaign to his immigrant parents' journey. Hilton, a former Fox News commentator and adviser to ex-British Prime Minister David Cameron, was endorsed by President Trump in April. That helped him pull ahead of Riverside County Sheriff Chad Bianco, the other major Republican. Hilton, who became a U.S. citizen five years ago, told supporters in Huntington Beach that 'change is coming to California and it's long overdue.' Steyer spent more than $213 million of his own money on a progressive, populist campaign. He remained confident late Tuesday, saying, 'We're going to wait until every ballot is counted. We're gonna give democracy a time to work.' The early results could shift because of unusual voting patterns: Republicans were more likely to vote early by mail, while many Democrats held onto their ballots or voted in person—a reversal of recent trends. The race was also shaped by who didn't run. High-profile Democrats like former Vice President Kamala Harris and U.S. Sen. Alex Padilla passed on the race. It was further disrupted in April when then-U.S. Rep. Eric Swalwell's campaign imploded amid sexual assault allegations, which he denied. His exit appeared to benefit Becerra. The winner will lead the nation's most populous state, a position that often carries national political prominence. Incumbent Gavin Newsom is term-limited and could seek the presidency.
why_it_matters: California's policies on climate, tech regulation, and immigration often set trends for the entire country, and its governor can become a presidential candidate; the outcome could shape issues like online privacy and education funding that directly affect young people nationwide.

background_read: California adopted its 'jungle primary' format in 2010, putting all candidates on one ballot; the top two finishers, regardless of party, advance to the November general election. This system was intended to favor moderate candidates but can produce same-party runoffs. Xavier Becerra is a former U.S. Health and Human Services Secretary under President Biden and was the first Latino to hold that cabinet post. Steve Hilton co-founded a major political consultancy and advised UK Prime Minister David Cameron during the Brexit era. Billionaire Tom Steyer, a former hedge fund manager, has poured his fortune into environmental activism and progressive campaigns. The eventual winner will replace Gavin Newsom, who has been governor since 2019 and is term-limited, meaning the state constitution prevents him from seeking a third consecutive term. California, with roughly 39 million residents, has the country's largest economy, and its governors—like Ronald Reagan before his presidency—often become national political figures. Eric Swalwell, a Democratic congressman known for his work on the House Intelligence Committee, saw his campaign implode in April.

perspectives.description: Becerra's supporters see his rise as an immigrant success story and a chance for progressive leadership; Hilton's backers believe a Republican can finally bring fiscal discipline and change to a state dominated by Democrats.
Critics fear the crowded field and top-two system could disenfranchise voters by limiting genuine choices, and the focus on personal wealth and celebrity endorsements undermines substantive debate.

California's jungle primary was designed to reduce partisanship, but it often produces unpredictable results; the race reflects a national trend of outsiders and wealthy candidates challenging traditional party structures.

If a Republican like Hilton advances, it could signal a shift in California politics and affect the 2028 presidential landscape; if two Democrats advance, the state's one-party rule will continue to shape national policy debates.
